Hongkong, Saturday, July 4, 1925.
REGISTRATION

hitherto responsible for lesser skilled work had been (unknowingly, of course) re-engaged by the police as coolies to relieve the situation at the docks and godowns occasioned a certain amount of resentment.
Those upon whom devolves the duty of selection among the crowds of coolies daily congregating at the police headquarters in the hope of being assigned work at the appointed scale of wages consider that they are entitled to more confidence in their ability to select between the good and the bad sheep. Their claim is not without justification in view of their long experience of that particular type of Chinese mentality—a glance at the hands and features and an experienced officer would probably be able to tell at once whether a man was, for instance, a dock hand or a scavenger, coolie. But such methods are after all not infallible, and unless some scheme of registration is introduced there will always be the possibility of strikers from a poorly paid service seeking more remunerative work which in addition guarantees them police protection on the spot.
Such a scheme of registration might even be extended to more highly skilled grades of labour for the purpose of distinguishing strikers and workers. Certificates, with photographs of their rightful owners attached, might be deemed impracticable; but something certainly ought to be done to draw a distinguishing line between those who are helping in this time of crisis and those whose presence is but a burden.

It is said that in 1918 a certain Government—Department frequently addressed envelopes to "Lloyd's Coffee House, Royal Exchange, E. C." The Royal Exchange had no obvious connection with an obscure little coffee house, in Great Tower Street, at the end of the 17th century, owned by one Edward Lloyd. Lloyd was a man of remarkable gifts, combining, journalistic ability with commercial enterprise. The result of his life-work is the great institution named after him, which is a byword in our language, and one of the most important insurance undertakings in the world. The cups of coffee sipped by the seventeenth century merchants over their news sheets, have, given place to luncheons in the Captains' Room, and the suggestion that this sanctum should be profaned by the overcrowded clerical staff, made it evident to the Members that Lloyds would have to migrate. As a result the King has just laid the foundation, in Leadenhall Street, of one of the most imposing buildings in the new London which is now rising around us. Designed by Sir Edwin Cooper, it will cost over one million pounds. Lloyds underwriters paid a larger sum for the "Lutine" Bell, which is sounded when news of a shipwreck is received. By an interesting coincidence the name of "Lutine" was brought up last week in an Old Bailey trial. The "Lutine" was captured from the French by Admiral Bacon in 1799, and later was loaned from the Admiralty, and sent, with £1,175,000 in bullion, from Yarmouth Broads to Hamburg. She mysteriously disappeared in the Zuyder Zee. Lloyds underwriters paid up at once, and in less than two weeks, the precious freight was again on its way. Divers have only succeeded in obtaining from the wreck some £30,000, a few cannon, and the famous bell.

TO PRESERVE PEACE IN EUROPE

(Reuter's American Service.)
At Henley in the semi-final of the Diamond Sculls, J. Beresford beat W. Hoover (America) by three lengths. Time: 8 minutes, 27 seconds.
Cambridge, (Mass.), July 3.

President Coolidge, speaking at a patriotic celebration, pledged the United States' moral support to the security pacts in order to preserve peace in Europe. He added that on no other terms could America be expected to contribute further to the financial revival of the old world.
In the other semi-final, D. Gollan beat M. Detton (France) by two lengths. Time: 9 minutes.
DOSSERS' TRIAL

London, July 3.—A strike has been declared at Tangier in protest against the financial provisions. The new regime is generally observed except by the French, who by keeping the shops open have infourred the hostility of the starters who smashed windows, providing a service from the store more covert. COUNSEL'S OBJECTIONS OVER-RULED.
(Reuter's Service.)

In the Mixed Court before the Chinese Magistrate and the British Assessor, Mr. Fischer, Counsel for Mr. and Mrs. Dosser, applied for at least a fortnight's remand on the grounds that the first charge (of making preparations to commit a hostile action against certain Foreign States) was incomplete and did not specify the countries; likewise the second and third charges were incomplete because no dates were mentioned.
[The'second and third' charges were of possessing literature likely to cause a breach of the peace and menacing the order of the Foreign Settlement.]
The Court replied that the Shanghai Municipal Police was an international body whose duty was to protect all nations. Therefore the objections would be overruled.

Mr. Fischer then challenged the Court's jurisdiction, pointing out that since the Revolution the Consular Body had appointed the Chinese Mixed Court Magistrates and entirely controlled the Mixed Court, consequently the Chinese Government did not recognise the Mixed Court as in Chinese Court; while by the Sino-Russian agreement of October 1924, Soviet citizens in China must be tried by the Chinese Court. Therefore the Mixed Court had no jurisdiction over the Dossers.

The Court again overruled Mr. Fischer's objection, the British Assessor stating that he had the most definite instructions from the Consular body with regard to hearing all Russian cases, criminal and civil.
Mr. Fischer's third plen was that he had not received all relevant documents from the police. The Court replied that the documents which he had not received would not be admitted for hearing to-day.

Inspector Yorke gave evidence of arrest, and described the documents found in the luggage of the accused, also a telegram which Dosser handed to the Captain of the steamship Mantua, informing the Soviet Consul at Shanghai that he was de-tained in Hongkong to be forcibly deported to Shanghai, and adding an urgent request that Peking should be informed. The Captain refused to wireless this message. The hearing was adjourned until Monday.
"LABOUR DUPES."
(Router's Service.)

Commenting on Chicherin's attack on Lord Birkenhead a leading article in the "Daily News" remarks that it does not know the value of Chicherin's denials regarding the Communist intervention in China. The main difficulty in the controversy about the question of propaganda is doubt as to how far the Soviets can control it even if they wished to do so.
A “Times” leader says that the causes, the extent, and the true character of the movement in China may be broadly ascribed to the contracts of the civilisations of East and West, which the progress of the world has rendered inevitable. A limited but influential class of Chinese, educated on Western lines have become acutely sensible to its existence. Upon this sensibility Bolshevism is playing with its accustomed flexibility. As the British Empire is admittedly the first principal bulwark of historic civilisation against the onslaught of world revolution, it is essential to the survival of Bolshevism that Muscovite politicians should direct the movement in China more particularly against the British, while assuring their Labour dupes in England that the Chinese agitators are revolting against Foreign Imperialism and Foreign Capitalism.

London, July 3.

At Wimbledon in the British Open Lawn Tennis Championship, the final of the ladies' singles, Mlle. Suzanne Lenglen beat Miss Joan Fry (England) 6-2, 6-0.
[Last year Suzanne Lenglen gave up towards the semi-final stage on doctor's orders and Miss K. McKane won in the final. This year Mlle. Lenglen defeated the English lady easily. Miss Joan Fry is one of the younger British players who came to the front this year by virtue of beating Miss McKane in one of the smaller championships before Wimbledon.]
There were extraordinary scenes. The queue since dawn was enormous. The weather was showery. The final was delayed 25 minutes owing to rain.

Miss Fry scored only 22 points. It was remarkable that her hitherto wonderful forehand was made to appear weak though her reputedly weak backhand was very sound. Suzanne was almost motionless and kept her opponent running to and fro on the baseline by superb placing. Miss Fry's wonderful nobility was a feature of the match. She kept up rallies but Mlle. Lenglen eventually made her over-hit and Miss Fry was at her mercy in the second set. The sets occupied 15 and 12 minutes, respectively.
In the semi-final of the ladies' doubles, Mlle. Lenglen (France) and Miss Ryan (U.S.A.) beat Mrs. Beamish and Miss Clarke 6-0, 6-2. [The winners meet Mrs. Bridge
The ladies' doubles match was very tame. Suzanne played with her usual excellence: Mrs. Beamish and Miss Clarke were outclassed.
In the semi-final of the men's doubles, Jean Borotra and R. Lacoste (France) beat De Morpurgo and Kehrlinger 11-9, 7-9, 6-1, 6-1.

This was a fierce battle of volleying with all four at the net. Borotra was once hitting the ball clean through the net; the referee awarded him the point. The fact was not discovered till the end of the game whereupon a new net was erected. Borotra and Kehrling stood out in their play; the former sometimes smashed from the baseline. The pace slowed down after the gruelling first and second sets with the continental pair deteriorating. Lacoste served brilliantly throughout.
It appears that.Borotra's through-the-net shot would have given their opponents the first set as the latter were leading 5-4 and 40-love.

Also in the semi-final of the men's doubles, John Hennessey and Ray Casey (U.S.A.) beat Brugnon and Cochet (France) 7-5, 5-7, 9-7, 6-4.
[In America last year, Hennessy beat Borotra, G. L. Patterson and B. I. C. Norton. Casey is somewhat like McLoughlin, the first American tennis "Comet." He is making his debut into international tennis.]

The American v. French match was a ding-dong struggle. The first four games went against the server; thereafter Cassey got into stride with his hurricane service and the games went to 5 all. The second set was almost a repetition of the first. The third set produced brilliant net-play, with racquet to racquet volleying. The fourth set was won from 4 all. Hennessey excelled in his forehand and Cassey in service; the French were superior in overhead work.

FRENCH BUDGET.
(Router's Sermico)
Paris July 8

The Chamber of Deputies has adopted the budget, fixing the expenditure for 1925 at 33,168,000,000 francs and the revenue at 33,175,000,000. M. Callaux suffered two minor reverses in the debate, firstly the Chamber rejecting the tax on the turnover of foodstuffs from other retailers, recommending the substitution of a tax on sugar, cocoa, coffee, tea, rice, coal and meat; secondly, fixing the cost of foreigners' identity tickets at two hundred francs as compared with fourteen as at present.

The debate lasted all night and was sometimes heated, notably the discussion of the cabinet proposal that the Government share the gross receipts of certain financial corporations, a suggestion which was adopted.
